item.text: {"chapter_id":"3B","question_ids":["3B.6","3B.7","3B.8","3B.9","3B.10"],"lens_quality":[{"question_id":"3B.6","factual_support_1_to_5":3,"completeness_1_to_5":3,"balance_1_to_5":4,"attribution_and_period_1_to_5":3,"judge_usefulness_1_to_5":4,"material_errors":["The 17.3% homicide decline is described as part of the 2018–2023 record, but BATCH-0016-E009 calculates it using AMLO’s final twelve months through September 2024, not a 2023 endpoint.","The answer cites BATCH-0016-E005 for military-execution allegations even though that ID is absent from its contrary-or-qualifying list; conversely, BATCH-0051-E017 and BATCH-0047-E009 appear in that list without being used in the answer. This weakens traceability.","The statement that reported crime rose 15.9% from 2022 to 2023 is supported, but describing this as deterioration in the target year should be qualified because the underlying survey/administrative measures do not all share identical event-year definitions.","The QCA result is reported accurately but given disproportionate inferential weight. It is a four-case controlled minimization and does not establish the causal effect of the National Guard nationally."],"material_omissions":["The full index contains material contrary evidence that serious human-rights violations and armed confrontations declined in absolute terms under AMLO, while excessive-force cases and weak accountability persisted (BATCH-0047-E009).","The answer omits the government’s formal rights-oriented security program and the Guardia Nacional’s express duties concerning proportional force, torture, arbitrary detention, assistance to victims, and detention registration (BATCH-0044-E011; BATCH-0057-E014; BATCH-0057-E015). These do not prove enforcement but matter to the lawful-means inquiry.","It omits direct 2023 accountability evidence, including civilian charges or investigations following Nuevo Laredo incidents and the State Department’s finding that the government generally took credible steps to identify and punish some abusive officials (BATCH-0004-E012; BATCH-0004-E013; BATCH-0012-E012; BATCH-0049-E005).","Communal and insurgent violence receive virtually no direct treatment, despite the lens expressly requiring them; the answer acknowledges the gap but does not inventory relevant candidate evidence.","The answer does not fully use the candidate index’s spending and institutional-capacity evidence showing a large shift toward military institutions and away from civilian security institutions (BATCH-0016-E007)."]},{"question_id":"3B.7","factual_support_1_to_5":4,"completeness_1_to_5":3,"balance_1_to_5":4,"attribution_and_period_1_to_5":4,"judge_usefulness_1_to_5":4,"material_errors":["BATCH-0015-E016 supports 80 strengthened laws through a UN/EU initiative coordinated with federal, state, and municipal actors; calling these simply administration-supported measures is defensible but should more clearly preserve the initiative’s external and subnational authorship.","The statement that UN agencies delivered thousands of shelter, education, nutrition, and protection interventions is accurate, but these outputs are not evidence that the administration itself funded or enforced protection; the answer later qualifies this, though the opening still risks over-crediting the state.","The answer says Amnesty documented approximately eleven women killed daily, which BATCH-0051-E009 supports, but it conflates all killings of women with femicides in the surrounding sentence. The evidence distinguishes women murdered from cases investigated as feminicides."],"material_omissions":["It omits major candidate-index evidence on legal advances in abortion, same-sex marriage, gender recognition, disability legal capacity, accessible shelters, and older-person protections (BATCH-0003-E007; BATCH-0003-E013). These are not sufficient protection outcomes but are relevant formal protections.","It omits evidence that the federal journalist/defender protection mechanism lacked staff or funding, operated sluggishly, and failed to protect some enrolled people, despite journalists and defenders being vulnerable groups under this lens (BATCH-0003-E006; BATCH-0003-E012; BATCH-0011-E004; BATCH-0018-E004).","It omits the 2023 killing or disappearance of nine journalists and 21 defenders contained in the very UN source used for positive measures (BATCH-0015-E016).","It omits direct 2023 CNDH migration evidence documenting improper returns, cruel treatment, detention, due-process violations, and 37 recommendations (BATCH-0021-R01-E014).","It omits direct evidence concerning the displaced El Bosque community’s alleged mistreatment, lack of food and water, stalled relocation, and inadequate services (BATCH-0044-E009).","Coverage of children outside migration, Afro-Mexicans, LGBT+ people outside detention, people with disabilities outside detention, and regional equity remains thin relative to the full candidate index."]},{"question_id":"3B.8","factual_support_1_to_5":3,"completeness_1_to_5":3,"balance_1_to_5":4,"attribution_and_period_1_to_5":4,"judge_usefulness_1_to_5":4,"material_errors":["The Guardia Nacional complaint-escalation and disciplinary procedures in BATCH-0057-E014 protect Guardia Nacional personnel facing internal discipline; they are not a public complaint, accountability, or remedy system for protesters. Presenting them alongside protest protections materially misleads the remedy inquiry.","The answer says the Guardia Nacional framework provided complaint escalation, disciplinary sanctions, hearings, defense, and appeals without identifying that these rights chiefly concern accused Guardia Nacional members rather than victims of excessive force.","The statement that Supreme Court invalidation of restrictive measures continued is broadly supported, but the cited online-rights decisions in BATCH-0026-E018 mostly date to 2022. Their period fit should be stated instead of presenting all as 2023 enforcement.","The answer treats press attacks as central evidence for protest and organization. They are relevant to dissent, but the lens also requires peaceful assembly, permit systems, policing orders, and remedies; those dimensions receive much less direct analysis."],"material_omissions":["It omits the favorable 2023 repeal of the 1917 Law on Printing Crimes by López Obrador (BATCH-0004-E014).","It omits the direct protest evidence that López Obrador called peaceful electoral-reform demonstrators allies of drug cartels and disparaged them as thieves (BATCH-0004-E014; BATCH-0012-E015).","It omits the candidate index’s Supreme Court rulings invalidating military control of the Guardia Nacional and an under-specified undercover-operation power, both material judicial checks on coercive enforcement (BATCH-0055-E006; BATCH-0055-E008; BATCH-0057-E006).","It omits CNDH and other oversight outputs relevant to actual remedies, including recommendations, acceptance rates, compliance evidence, and measures for journalists and defenders (BATCH-0021-R01-E004; BATCH-0021-R01-E009; BATCH-0021-R01-E015).","It does not examine the twelve state laws restricting demonstrations, applicable permit systems, geographic variation in protest policing, or whether victims obtained compensation or full reparation.","The 19.4% year-on-year decline in documented press aggression and ARTICLE 19’s warning that underreporting may explain part of it are omitted, reducing balance within the press evidence itself."]},{"question_id":"3B.9","factual_support_1_to_5":4,"completeness_1_to_5":2,"balance_1_to_5":4,"attribution_and_period_1_to_5":4,"judge_usefulness_1_to_5":3,"material_errors":["The formal national security program and general constitutional standards for military policing are not evidence that Hurricane Otis or another 2023 crisis response actually complied with restraint, proportionality, or independent supervision. The answer acknowledges this but still gives these general rules substantial space.","BATCH-0055-E012 concerns public-security collaboration, not disaster relief. Its relevance to Hurricane Otis is indirect and should not be presented as a crisis-response safeguard without evidence connecting it to the operation.","The claim of 'restoration of power and communications' is too broad. BATCH-0003-E022 reports 99% electricity restoration and 70% telephone-network restoration as of November 8, not complete restoration of both.","The phrase 'incomplete information' is supportable from the cited reporting, but the answer understates the more specific AP evidence that some officials were not permitted to provide casualty or search details and that AMLO accused critics of wanting a high death toll to blame his government."],"material_omissions":["The answer omits direct Otis evidence that the emergency declaration initially covering 47 municipalities was rectified to only two municipalities, a potentially material allocation and exposure issue in BATCH-0003-E022.","It omits BATCH-0029-E003, which directly documents AMLO’s delayed road journey, short stay, and return before services and a damage report were available. The item is included in the candidate index and even listed among contrary evidence elsewhere, but is absent from the answer.","It omits direct 2023 evidence on the El Bosque displacement crisis, including alleged mistreatment, a day without food or water, stalled relocation, homelessness, and inadequate services (BATCH-0044-E009).","It omits the IAEA preparedness evidence on prior emergency exercises, identified weaknesses, and delayed follow-up (BATCH-0002-E010), which is relevant contextual evidence for preparedness although not direct Otis performance.","The answer does not address whether the government’s decision not to appeal for international assistance affected protective resource allocation (BATCH-0003-E022).","It gives no sustained assessment of warning, evacuation, casualty-information transparency, search operations, distribution across poor neighborhoods, or corrective action after early failures.","The direct public-messaging evidence is underdeveloped: AMLO’s statements accusing critics of exaggerating deaths are material to the censorship/correction side of the lens and warrant explicit assessment.","Ayotzinapa and Nuevo Laredo add little to this crisis lens compared with omitted direct disaster and displacement evidence; their inclusion displaces more probative candidate-index material."]},{"question_id":"3B.10","factual_support_1_to_5":3,"completeness_1_to_5":3,"balance_1_to_5":4,"attribution_and_period_1_to_5":3,"judge_usefulness_1_to_5":4,"material_errors":["The answer cites BATCH-0016-E009 for a 17.3% homicide decline as part of a 2018–2023 comparison, but that figure uses AMLO’s final twelve months through September 2024. It should not be characterized as a 2023 endpoint.","The 111,540 registry figure is cumulative from 1962 through September 2023, not disappearances occurring during AMLO’s period. The phrase 'reported disappearances reached' is technically possible but risks implying an administration-period flow rather than a cumulative stock.","The statement that 'reported crime' reversed from 2022 to 2023 should specify the underlying measure and its survey/administrative timing; the answer combines indicators with different reference periods.","The answer says prison overcrowding, violence, complaints, and weak remedies continued while citing BATCH-0049-E011 and BATCH-0016-E010. These sources support the general proposition, but some prison findings are facility-specific and some trends span 2018–2023, so the national end-state phrasing should be more carefully bounded.","The supporting-evidence list omits several IDs used for favorable propositions in the prose and classifies the evidence awkwardly: BATCH-0049-E011 is mixed rather than simply supporting, while BATCH-0004-E019 is both favorable and adverse."],"material_omissions":["It omits the full index’s strongest administration-wide end-state evidence: México Evalúa’s explicit conclusion that AMLO left a more violent and equally impune country with fewer institutional capacities, while also listing concrete positive results (BATCH-0016-E012). The answer cites it but does not clearly distinguish source judgment from independently verified outcomes.","It omits direct evidence that 2023 National Human Rights Commission recommendations included both inherited and current-administration grave violations, along with partial acceptance and compliance (BATCH-0021-R01-E008; BATCH-0021-R01-E009).","It omits the countervailing WOLA evidence of reduced absolute levels of torture, enforced disappearances, extrajudicial executions, and armed confrontations compared with earlier periods (BATCH-0047-E009).","It omits direct evidence on the weakening or closure of disappearance and identification capacity, registry revision, and presidential claims that missing-person totals were exaggerated (BATCH-0003-E005; BATCH-0003-E011; BATCH-0004-E008).","It omits substantial end-state evidence concerning journalist and defender safety, protection-mechanism weakness, military surveillance, and self-censorship, which are material to reporting freedom and the reliability of apparent safety trends (BATCH-0003-E006; BATCH-0003-E012; BATCH-0012-E007; BATCH-0014-E006).","It does not clearly separate the 2023 annual assessment from the broader 2018–2024 ruler-period assessment, despite relying on both kinds of evidence.","It does not give a sufficiently explicit inherited-to-end comparison for state violence: inherited military abuse and impunity were severe, but AMLO expanded military authority and failed to establish consistently effective civilian accountability."]}],"verdict":"pass_with_corrections","strengths":["All five answers preserve meaningful favorable and adverse evidence instead of treating low crime, formal law, or high reporting volume as dispositive.","The answers generally distinguish federal presidential responsibility from state, municipal, criminal, UN, and civil-society roles.","The treatment of underreporting, cifra negra, disappearance methodology, inherited violence, organized-crime fragmentation, and external firearms supply is useful to a skeptical judge.","The answers usually distinguish formal reforms and institutional capacity from demonstrated enforcement, remedy, or nationwide outcomes.","The prose correctly avoids claiming direct presidential orders for local abuses or individual military incidents without evidence."],"systemic_problems":["The answers do not systematically test themselves against the complete candidate index; several high-value favorable and adverse items are omitted despite being directly relevant.","Period handling is inconsistent, especially the repeated use of a 17.3% homicide comparison ending in September 2024 as though it were a 2018–2023 result.","Citation envelopes are not fully auditable: some prose-cited IDs are absent from the evidence lists, some listed IDs are unused, and mixed evidence is forced into supporting-versus-contrary categories.","Formal legal safeguards are sometimes given weight outside their proper scope. The clearest example is treating internal Guardia Nacional disciplinary rights as a public remedy for protesters.","The answers sometimes combine annual 2023 evidence, lagged 2022 surveys, administration-wide evidence, and post-2023 retrospective evidence without sufficiently explicit temporal labeling.","Question 3B.9 is especially under-complete: it relies on general security doctrine and contextual accountability cases while omitting direct crisis, displacement, preparedness, allocation, and presidential-response evidence.","The answers identify important uncertainty but do not consistently state which omitted or unresolved item could materially change a future judgment."],"concrete_corrections_required":["Correct every reference to the 17.3% homicide decline to state that the comparison ends in September 2024, or remove it from a 2023-only assessment.","For 3B.8, remove the suggestion that Guardia Nacional internal complaint and disciplinary procedures provide victims or protesters with accountability and remedy; describe their actual scope precisely.","For 3B.9, add BATCH-0003-E022’s disaster-declaration narrowing, BATCH-0029-E003’s presidential travel and short stay, BATCH-0044-E009’s El Bosque displacement response, and the specific AP evidence on poor-area distribution and casualty messaging.","For 3B.7, distinguish killings of women from cases classified or investigated as femicides, and add omitted protection-mechanism, disability, LGBT+, abortion, journalist/defender, and direct CNDH migration evidence.","For 3B.6 and 3B.10, add the countervailing evidence of reduced absolute serious abuses and confrontations from BATCH-0047-E009, while preserving its warnings about militarization and weak accountability.","Label cumulative disappearance totals explicitly as registry stocks since 1962, not target-period incident counts.","Reconcile every evidence-ID array with the prose: include every cited ID, remove unused IDs, and treat mixed sources as mixed rather than forcing them into a single polarity.","Separate 2023-only findings, lagged survey findings, administration-wide findings, and post-period retrospective findings in each answer.","Add a brief complete-index coverage statement to each answer identifying the most material considered-but-unused evidence and why it was excluded or treated as duplicative."],"safe_for_judge_use":false,"rationale":"The answers are substantively useful and generally balanced, but they are not yet safe as a complete judge-facing evidence synthesis. The recurring 2024 endpoint error, the mischaracterization of internal Guardia Nacional disciplinary procedures as relevant public remedy, inconsistent citation lists, and material omissions from the full candidate index require correction. Question 3B.9 is notably incomplete, while the other four can become judge-usable through targeted period, scope, and coverage repairs."}
